q: What kind of horsepower numbers does this thing put down on a dyno?
topic: FC 350 2019 dyno, weight and power feel
statement: On a magazine dyno the 2019 FC 350 made 53.30 hp at peak and 50.82 hp near 10,000 rpm, against 48.76 hp there for the 2018 engine. It weighed 222 lb. It is snappy off idle, calmer in the middle and surges past 8,000 rpm to a 13,400 rpm limiter, so it should not be short-shifted. Testers raced on map two.

q: Just curious, how much power does my bike actually make?
statement: On a magazine dyno the 2012-2014 150 SX made 38.81-38.83 hp at 11,100 rpm, about 4 hp more than the 125 SX. It weighed 205-206.5 lb. The powerband is narrow and it only makes speed when ridden hard. List price $6,599 in 2014.

q: What kind of horsepower numbers does this thing put down on a dyno?
topic: CRF450R 2019 dyno, weight and price against the class
statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2019 CRF450R made 60.21 hp peak and 36.25 lb-ft at 7,500 rpm, with 37.52 hp at 6,000 rpm, 54.67 at 8,000 and 59.71 at 10,000, the most in the class. It weighed 238 lb without fuel and listed at $9,299.

q: Just curious, how much power does my bike actually make?
statement: On a magazine dyno the 2014 CRF450R peaked at 51.97 hp and made 49.57 hp at 9,900 rpm, where the 2014 YZ450F made 58.22. It weighed 236 lb. Strong roll-on power up to about 8,500 rpm, then flat.

q: Just curious, how much power does my bike actually make?
topic: 450 SX-F 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 450 SX-F made 57.98 hp at 9,200 rpm and 36.63 lb-ft, the most of the six 450s on both counts: 38.63 hp at 6,000 rpm, 54.59 at 8,000 and 56.68 at 10,000. It stays above 50 hp from 7,200 to 11,500 rpm, the widest band in the class.

q: My buddy says his bike makes more power than mine. What does mine really make?
statement: On a magazine dyno the 2017 KX250F peaked at 40.06 hp (2017 YZ250F 40.93, Austrian 250s about 44) and revved to 13,400 rpm. Against the 2016 it was equal or down from 6,000-9,300 rpm, about 1 hp up from 9,500-11,500 rpm and softer off the bottom, so it can lose a bike length out of a turn and needs clutch if shifted early.

q: What kind of horsepower numbers does this thing put down on a dyno?
statement: On a magazine dyno the YZ125 peaked at 35.36 hp at 11,600 rpm and made 16.3 hp at 7,000 rpm. It picks up well from low to mid for a 125 and flattens on top, where the Austrian 125 of the same years pulls away; the rider has to work the clutch to keep it singing. It weighed 194 lb on a magazine scale in 2017 and listed at $6,499 in 2019.

q: Just curious, how much power does my bike actually make?
statement: On a second magazine's rear-wheel dyno the new 2019 KX450 made 52.63 hp at 9,480 rpm and 32.80 lb-ft at 6,730 rpm, with noticeably more power than the earlier engine in every part of the range. The engine has a 44 mm throttle body and larger titanium valves.

q: My buddy says his bike makes more power than mine. What does mine really make?
topic: 450 SX-F 2017 third-source dyno, fuelled weight and test notes
statement: A third outlet's 2017 450 test measured the 450 SX-F (the mid-year Factory Edition) at 52.5 hp at 9,800 rpm on its rear-wheel dyno and 236.3 lb fully fuelled, the lightest in the test, with the best brakes. To cure headshake the testers took eight clicks of compression out of the air fork. They preferred the stock map.

q: Just curious, how much power does my bike actually make?
topic: KX450 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 KX450F made 55.43 hp at 9,000 rpm, with 54.03 hp at 8,000 rpm and 51.55 at 10,000. The midrange is solid and the top end fades; it stays above 50 hp for 2,800 rpm, fifth of six.

q: My buddy says his bike makes more power than mine. What does mine really make?
topic: 250 SX-F 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 250 SX-F made 43.79 hp at 13,900 rpm and 20.20 lb-ft: 29.46 hp at 8,000 rpm, 36.49 at 10,000 and 43.79 at 12,000. It is a high-rpm engine that holds over 37 hp across a long band.

q: What kind of horsepower numbers does this thing put down on a dyno?
statement: On a magazine dyno the 2010 YZ250F (and the unchanged 2011) made 35.88 hp at 11,500 rpm and 18.95 lb-ft. It is very quick off the bottom and best from low to mid, with little pull above about 9,500 rpm. It measured 95.5 dB.

q: What kind of horsepower numbers does this thing put down on a dyno?
statement: On a magazine dyno the 2012 CRF450R made 52.59 hp, the lowest of the five Japanese and Austrian 450s that year, and weighed 231 lb without fuel, 7-13 lb less than its rivals. Tractable and easy to ride, flat above about 8,600 rpm. An aftermarket exhaust added about 2.5 hp at peak in testing.

q: Just curious, how much power does my bike actually make?
topic: FC 250 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 FC 250 made 44.38 hp at 13,900 rpm and 20.73 lb-ft, the highest peak in the class: 29.58 hp at 8,000 rpm, 36.60 at 10,000 and 44.23 at 12,000. It needs high rpm to make its power.

q: Just curious, how much power does my bike actually make?
statement: On a magazine dyno the 250 SX-F made 36.41 hp at 10,800 rpm and 19.96 lb-ft in 2011, and 35.52 hp at 10,800 rpm and 19.43 lb-ft in 2012. With the electric starter added for 2012 it weighed 231 lb, the heaviest 250 four-stroke of its year. More bottom and middle than the carburetted 2010 but slow to rev and soft off idle.

q: What kind of horsepower numbers does this thing put down on a dyno?
statement: On a magazine dyno the 2012 and 2013 CRF250R made 38.44 hp at 11,000 rpm and 20.0 lb-ft, holding over 38 hp from 10,300 to 11,300 rpm and 35.60 hp at 13,200 rpm. The 2012 weighed 222 lb, the lightest fuel-injected 250 four-stroke of its year. Midrange-led with a surge from 6,500 to 7,700 rpm.

q: Just curious, how much power does my bike actually make?
statement: On a magazine dyno the 2019 CRF250R peaked at 42.40 hp (2018: 40.68), about 2 hp up from 8,000 to 10,000 rpm. It weighed 228 lb. Still linear and weak from low to mid; it pulls hardest from about 10,000 rpm up.

q: Just curious, how much power does my bike actually make?
topic: CRF450R 2018 third-source dyno and engine notes
statement: A third outlet's 2018 450 test measured the CRF450R at 52.9 hp at 9,300 rpm and 33.2 lb-ft at 7,700 rpm: a strong low-end burst and torque that arrives early, with the heaviest clutch pull in the class. One test bike stalled several times and was hard to restart.

q: Was my bike any good compared to the competition that year? What did the magazines think?
topic: CRF250R 2019 full-tank weight and third-opinion ranking
statement: A third magazine ranked the 2019 CRF250R fourth of six: good suspension, comfortable ergonomics and the nimblest handling in the test. It weighed 239 lb with a full tank, the heaviest of the five.

q: Was my bike any good compared to the competition that year? What did the magazines think?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2018 KX450F fifth of six: linear, usable low-to-mid power and predictable handling, but about 2.5 hp down on the leaders with no reason to rev past about 8,800 rpm. The clutch slips (stiffer springs), the chain guide wears fast (aftermarket guide), the air forks are dated and it benefits from new mapping.

q: Was my bike any good compared to the competition that year? What did the magazines think?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2015 YZ125 first of three 125s: the best suspension in the class, a broad, easy powerband, a balanced chassis and a close-ratio six-speed. It gives up top-end power to the Austrian bikes, the front brake is modest and the clutch is cable-operated. An oversized front disc was their first purchase.

q: Where did my bike land in the shootouts for its year, and why?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2015 FC 250 fifth of six despite more than 43 hp, a hydraulic clutch, a strong front brake and a two-position map switch. The airbox dulls throttle response, the suspension stays stiff and the power is all on top. Their fixes: drain 10 cc from each fork leg, drill the airbox cover (and clean the filter more often), raise the fork legs 15 mm and run 105 mm of sag.

q: Where did my bike land in the shootouts for its year, and why?
statement: In a magazine's 2016 250 shootout the FC 250 made the most power and torque, 44.38 hp at 13,900 rpm, at 223 lb, with broad power, strong brakes and an excellent hydraulic clutch. The plastic airbox dulls throttle response and slows how quickly it revs, and it is 2 lb heavier than the KTM.

q: Was my bike any good compared to the competition that year? What did the magazines think?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2018 CRF450R tied for second of six: a hard-hitting midrange, sharp turn-in, cleaner running on the new map and electric start, at 240 lb. Weak points: the seven-plate clutch with its judder spring breaks plates (replace the judder-spring set with an extra plate), slow-reacting brakes, forks that chatter over small bumps and dive on big hits, and no traction or launch control. The crew also ran stiffer springs, new mapping and a higher-pressure radiator cap.

q: Where did my bike land in the shootouts for its year, and why?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2018 FC 250 second of six at 220 lb: strong top-end, plush air forks and a forgiving feel. The plastic airbox chokes low and mid power, the gearing is too tall and the stock map lacks bottom-end: drill the left airbox cover and fit a 13-tooth countershaft sprocket.

q: How did my bike stack up against the others in its class when it was new?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2013 YZ450F fifth of six: 55.24 hp at 9,100 rpm and 238 lb, with the top-rated fork and shock and very good durability. The powerband is disjointed, turn-in is flawed, the radiator wings are wide and the airbox is noisy.

q: How did my bike stack up against the others in its class when it was new?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2012 CRF250R fourth of five: 38.44 hp at 11,000 rpm, 222 lb, $7,420, with a strong midrange and a new linkage that settles the rear. The frame geometry brings oversteer and headshake, the forks dive under braking, the springs are too soft for riders over 165 lb and the exhaust holds back the top end.

q: Was my bike any good compared to the competition that year? What did the magazines think?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2016 CRF450R fifth of six at 233 lb: lively off the bottom, tractable and predictable for local racers, with longer forks that calmed the front at speed. It has the least power and torque in the class, a spongy clutch, an air fork they rated poorly and a shock spring too soft for riders over 190 lb.

q: Where did my bike land in the shootouts for its year, and why?
topic: KX250 2019 full-tank weight and third-opinion ranking
statement: A third magazine ranked the 2019 KX250 fifth of six and noted it was carried over from 2018 apart from graphics, shroud colour and the model name. It weighed 232 lb with a full tank.

q: Was my bike any good compared to the competition that year? What did the magazines think?
statement: A magazine crew narrowly ranked the 2015 YZ250 first of three 250 two-strokes on the balance of suspension, power delivery, comfort and reliability, even though it was the weakest on the dyno, the slowest off the line and had the weakest brakes. Stock jetting runs clean on pump fuel and changes tend to make it lean. Raising the fork in the clamps with about 107 mm of sag helped cornering at the cost of high-speed stability. The clutch needed frequent adjustment.

q: Was my bike any good compared to the competition that year? What did the magazines think?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2018 450 SX-F first of six 450s: the lightest (19 lb under the heaviest), with a long, usable powerband, the strongest brakes, a self-adjusting hydraulic clutch, accurate handling, precise shifting, air forks that work across rider weights and working launch and traction control. They listed no weaknesses.

q: Was my bike any good compared to the competition that year? What did the magazines think?
topic: 250 SX-F 2019 second-opinion shootout notes and wet weight
statement: A second magazine ranked the 2019 250 SX-F first of six: the complete package, with the smoothest gearbox in the group and an air fork that needed fewer changes than the Husqvarna's. Listed wet weight 232 lb, $8,999. Most testers preferred the aggressive map.

q: How did my bike stack up against the others in its class when it was new?
statement: In a magazine's 2016 125 shootout the new 125 SX beat the YZ125 on power: 37.27 hp against 34.01, with about two more horsepower low down, from an engine 4 lb lighter than before. It has a self-adjusting hydraulic clutch and a tool-free air filter. The WP suspension has weak bottoming resistance and it stands up in corners as delivered; raising the fork legs 5 mm helps it settle at turn-in.

q: Was my bike any good compared to the competition that year? What did the magazines think?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2016 YZ450F fourth of six at 238 lb, 11 lb more than the lightest bike: excellent suspension, a strong pull above 9,000 rpm and proven reliability, but vague at turn-in and inclined to push in flat corners, with a weak clutch. Their setup: a 49-tooth rear sprocket in place of the 48, the fork raised in the clamps and 103 mm of sag.

q: Was my bike any good compared to the competition that year? What did the magazines think?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2017 FC 250 second of six: 44.38 hp, the highest peak, 220 lb and $8,599, with smooth, broad delivery. The moulded plastic airbox dulls throttle response; drilling it is the fix.

q: Where did my bike land in the shootouts for its year, and why?
statement: A magazine crew ranked the 2015 KX250F second of six on the broadest usable power in the class. It understeers and the shock wallows in corners (different offset clamps and a longer link arm), it resists shifting under load and the clutch does not last like the hydraulic ones (stiffer springs). Use the white coupler.

q: Was my bike any good compared to the competition that year? What did the magazines think?
statement: A second magazine found the 2013 CRF450R the lightest 450 at 106.8 kg with fluids but no fuel and the most agile, but short of low-rev torque and throttle response, with a restrictive exhaust. Adding a few psi to the air fork settled it at speed. Fork pressure rose 4-6 psi within half an hour of riding, so check it between sessions. For 2013 compression went from 12.0 to 12.5:1 and the tank from 5.7 to 6.3 litres.

q: How did my bike stack up against the others in its class when it was new?
statement: In a magazine's 2015 250 two-stroke shootout the TC 250 cornered best of the three, with a smooth powerband from its sealed airbox, but it lacks the KTM's midrange punch, the suspension is hard to balance and riders were less confident on big jumps. The aggressive map (setting two) worked best. Against the 250 SX it has wider, curved bars, a slipperier seat and less vibration.

q: I just picked this up used. What should I know about this model year?
statement: The 2013 450 SX-F had a new engine and frame with fuel injection, plain bearings, a larger rear axle and a one-piece swingarm. It made 56.95 hp on a magazine dyno and weighed 240 lb, 3 lb less than 2012. Known points: the exhaust cannot come off without removing the shock (aftermarket systems with a separate mid-pipe avoid this), the seat foam is soft, and the stock suspension was criticised.

q: I just picked this up used. What should I know about this model year?
statement: For 2015 the 450 SX-F changed from the bladder fork to the WP 4CS, with new rims and tyres, axle and steering-stem changes and less weight. Known points: the air filter cage can unseat, the shock needed a stiffer spring (the 2014 spring was preferred), and if the fork is not using its travel, lowering the oil by 10 cc helps.

q: Is this a good year of this bike to own? Anything it's known for?
statement: The 2011 450 SX-F was the first with rising-rate linkage rear suspension in place of the no-link system, in a smaller, slimmer package, at 242 lb. Known points: the radiator overflow could vent steam (cured with a longer vent hose routed under the cases), the nylon shock preload ring deforms and is hard to turn, and the spokes and rims need watching. Testers rated the handling and powerband highly.

q: Is this a good year of this bike to own? Anything it's known for?
statement: The 2018 450 SX-F kept the AER fork and gained two-piece lower bar clamps and a push-button map and launch-control switch; it made almost 58 hp at 222 lb. Known points: the bar clamps can twist and deform their rubbers, the map switch is hard to use with gloves, the fuel pump relay hangs loosely, and the fork air valve is hard to reach with a cap that is easily lost.

q: Is this a good year of this bike to own? Anything it's known for?
topic: CRF450R: which used year to buy (2017 against 2018)
statement: Magazine advice on used CRF450Rs: the 2017 is the better buy of the 2017-2018 pair. The 2017 weighs 233 lb and makes 57.49 hp but has no electric start. The 2018 added the starter and 7 lb with it, plus stiffer fork and shock springs and a revised map. A 2017 can be brought up to date with the dealer map update and a suspension shop setup, and 2018 head parts fit the 2017.

q: Is this a good year of this bike to own? Anything it's known for?
statement: A magazine's used-bike advice steers buyers away from the 2009-2016 CRF450R generations and towards the 2017-on bike, calling the earlier ones flawed. Anyone riding one should weigh that against price and condition.

q: I just picked this up used. What should I know about this model year?
statement: The 2016 450 SX-F was 7.9 lb lighter than 2015 at 227 lb, made close to 58 hp, and gained rubber-mounted bars and a tool-free air filter. Known points: the fuel cap sticks, the fork dives and bottoms for faster riders, the brake pedal spring can pop off (turn it round and crimp the tangs), and the downsized rectifier can fail, with the 2015 or 2017 part used as the replacement.

q: Is this a good year of this bike to own? Anything it's known for?
statement: The 2017 450 SX-F got the WP AER 48 air fork and launch control and weighed 222 lb. Known points: sprocket bolts and spokes need constant checking (one test wheel broke five front spokes), neutral is hard to find at a standstill, the front brake hose can crimp, the fork clicker is small, the fuel cap sticks and the exhaust still cannot come off without removing the shock.

q: Is this a good year of this bike to own? Anything it's known for?
statement: For 2012 the 450 SX-F got a diaphragm-spring (Belleville) clutch and a repositioned rear brake bleed hole. Tester fixes: the bars are too low (5 mm risers or bars 12-19 mm taller) and the gearing too tall (a 53-tooth rear sprocket was preferred). It is heavy for the class.

q: I just picked this up used. What should I know about this model year?
statement: For 2014 the 450 SX-F got a stiffer clutch spring, more fork compression damping and the 250 SX-F-style muffler. Known points: the rims are prone to loose spokes (stronger aftermarket rims were the cure), and the WP fork and shock fall short for heavier or faster riders, with a specialist fork rebuild suggested.

q: What jetting do people usually end up running on this bike?
topic: tuner jetting for the 250 (sea level, race fuel)
statement: A tuner runs the YZ250 one size leaner than stock: 175 main, 48 pilot, stock N3EW on the 2nd clip, air screw 1 turn, 50 power jet and a 7.0 slide, for race fuel at 0-1,500 ft and 70-85 F.

q: What jetting do people usually end up running on this bike?
statement: Jetting for the 2011-2012 450 SX-F (41 mm Keihin FCR): 185 main, 42 pilot, OBDTQ needle on the 6th clip from the top, 50 leak jet, fuel screw 1-3/4 turns out. If it will not fire on the starter, richen the fuel screw.

q: What jetting do people usually end up running on this bike?
statement: Tested jetting for the 2018 TC 250 (38 mm Mikuni TMX, 60:1 premix): 450 main (stock 440), 45 pilot (stock 42.5), 43-73 needle on the third clip, air screw 1/4 turn out (stock 1-1/2). Gearing: 14/49 in place of the stock 14/50; novices and vets may prefer one tooth more at the rear.

q: Is the stock jetting on my bike any good, or do most people change it?
statement: Jetting for the 2011-2019 YZ125 (38 mm Mikuni TMX): 430 main (a 440 and a 420 come with the bike), 40 pilot, 6BFY43-3 needle on the 3rd clip from the top, air screw 2-1/4 turns out. With porting or an aftermarket pipe go to the 440 main and add some race fuel to the mix for safety.

q: Is the stock jetting on my bike any good, or do most people change it?
statement: A magazine test crew's 2017 TC 250 setup: fork air 144 psi (it bottoms below that), compression 23 clicks out (stock 12), rebound 19 out (stock 12), legs at the second line. Shock 42 N/mm spring, 107 mm sag, high-speed compression 1-1/4 turns out (stock 2), low-speed 8 clicks out (stock 15), rebound 14 out (stock 15). Jetting (Mikuni TMX 38): 450 main (stock 440), 42.5 pilot, 43-73 needle on the 3rd clip, air screw 2-1/2 turns (stock 1). Rear sprocket 49 in place of 50; second to third is a short gap. Unplugging the white connector under the tank gives the mellow ignition map.

q: What jetting do people usually end up running on this bike?
statement: A magazine test crew's 2019 TC 250 setup: fork air 144 psi (stock 151), compression 32 clicks out (stock 15), rebound 15 out, legs at the first line (stock second); new forks need 2-4 hours to break in. Shock 42 N/mm spring, 105 mm sag, high-speed compression 1-1/2 turns out, low-speed 16 clicks out, rebound 14 out. Jetting: 450 main, 35 pilot, 6BFY43-71 needle on the 3rd clip, air screw 1-1/2 turns; the manual says 60:1 premix and it ran crispest there, though the crew preferred the protection of 40:1. Gearing 14/49 in place of 14/50. Power valve: counter-clockwise for more hit and top end, clockwise for a mellower bottom.

q: What jetting do people usually end up running on this bike?
statement: The 2017 TX 300 is rich as delivered. Stock Mikuni jetting: 430 main, 37.5 pilot, 44-73 needle on the third clip, air screw 1-1/2 turns out. Tested fix: 420 main, 35 pilot, 43-73 needle on the second clip, air screw 2 turns out, on 60:1 premix.

q: What jetting do people usually end up running on this bike?
statement: A magazine test crew's 2014 250 SX setup: fork 0.46 kg/mm springs, oil at 370 cc for vets and 390 cc for pros (stock 380), compression 7 clicks out (stock 12), rebound 12 out, legs 5 mm up. Shock 5.4 kg/mm spring (5.7 for faster or heavier riders), 105 mm sag, high-speed compression 2 turns out, low-speed 15 clicks out, with a link 1.25 mm longer (lowers the rear 10 mm and firms the first part of the stroke). Jetting: 158 main (160 in cool weather), 40 pilot (stock 42), N1EH needle on the 4th clip (stock 3rd), air screw 1-1/2 turns.

q: Is the stock gearing right for most riders on my bike?
statement: Stock gearing on the 2013-2016 CRF450R is 13/48 and testers found it tall for the low-to-mid power. They went to 13/49, or 14/52 for a ratio in between.

q: What gearing do people like on this bike?
statement: The 2017 450 XC-F has a close-ratio five-speed. Stock gearing tops out at 91 mph, and testers recommended re-gearing either way for tight trails or for fast desert, and wished for a sixth gear or wider spacing.

q: Is the stock gearing right for most riders on my bike?
topic: FE 350 and FE 501 street-legal versions: gearing and suspension (2015)
statement: On the 2015 street-legal FE models the 350 is the revver and is geared tall; a smaller countershaft sprocket gives it more snap at low speed. The 501 has torque everywhere and very long gearing. The 350 is the better balanced and plusher of the two. The 501 wants stiffer fork springs or more preload; adding compression balances it but costs plushness. Both have hard seats, weak stock batteries and no kickstarter (it was an accessory).

q: What gearing do people like on this bike?
topic: YZ250X gearbox and clutch vs YZ250 (sprocket equivalents)
statement: Compared with the YZ250, the YZ250X third gear is lower by about one rear-sprocket tooth, fourth is taller by about two teeth and fifth by about five teeth; its clutch springs are about 10% softer.

q: What gearing do people like on this bike?
statement: The YZ125 comes with a 48-tooth rear sprocket. Testers ran a 49 to sharpen second gear and reach third sooner.

q: How is my bike different from its sister models? I never really understood the lineup.
statement: Of the 2016 two-strokes, the TE 250 is the livelier, with smooth, predictable power, less vibration and a lighter feel. The TE 300 pulls harder from the bottom and needs less clutch in slow going. Both feel planted and are less likely to deflect off roots and rocks than the 125. Both have a two-map switch on the bar.

q: What sets my bike apart from the motocross version or the other models it's related to?
statement: The 2012-2015 150 SX is a 143.6 cc engine with a 56 x 58.4 mm bore and stroke (125 SX: 54 x 54.5 mm) and its own crank, cylinder, piston, power valve and pipe tuning. It has all-steel clutch plates with stiffer springs where the 125 uses aluminium, and 13/48 gearing against the 125's 13/50.

q: How is my bike different from its sister models? I never really understood the lineup.
topic: FE 350 2019: how it differs from the KTM 350
statement: The 2019 FE 350 shares its engine with the KTM 350 but uses linkage rear suspension (KTM: PDS), a composite airbox and subframe, Magura brake and clutch hydraulics (KTM: Brembo) and its own bodywork, with a WP Xplor 48 coil fork. The street-legal version weighed 243 lb without fuel and listed at $10,899. Its six-speed has a lower first than the competition model, the same second and taller gears above.

q: How is my bike different from its sister models? I never really understood the lineup.
statement: At 231 lb the 2018 KX450F was 8 lb lighter than the YZ450F and 9 lb lighter than the CRF450R on a magazine scale, and 9 lb heavier than the electric-start 450 SX-F. Its air fork is about 3 lb lighter than a comparable coil fork. A little decel pop remains, a sign it still runs slightly lean.

q: How is my bike different from its sister models? I never really understood the lineup.
topic: FE 350 2015: how it differs from the KTM 350 XCF-W
statement: The 2015 FE 350 shares its engine with the KTM 350 XCF-W from throttle body to muffler; only the airbox and boot differ. The chassis has linkage rear suspension where the KTM uses PDS, a WP 4CS closed-cartridge fork (compression on one leg, rebound on the other), a three-piece composite subframe, billet triple clamps, a tool-free air filter and no kickstarter. For 2015 it got new shrouds, front fender and headlight. It weighed 265 lb with a full 2.4-gallon tank, about 10 lb more than the XCF-W, and listed at $9,649.

q: How is my bike different from its sister models? I never really understood the lineup.
topic: 2016-2018 FC models against the KTM SX-F
statement: The 2016-2018 FC models share frame, engine, geometry and suspension hardware with the KTM SX-F and differ in: a three-piece composite subframe and airbox that is nearly sealed, a Magura hydraulic clutch (KTM uses Brembo), Pro Taper bars with a slightly lower, shorter bend, a seat about 5 mm lower, D.I.D DirtStar rims, heavier GFK brake discs, a muffler with internal cones where the KTM's is straight-through (FC 450), and their own suspension settings. They weigh about 2 lb more than the KTM and feel a little softer and more forgiving in the chassis.

q: What sets my bike apart from the motocross version or the other models it's related to?
topic: CRF450RX: how it differs from the CRF450R
statement: The CRF450RX is the CRF450R motocross bike set up for closed-course off-road racing. It adds electric start, a 2.2-gallon plastic tank in place of the titanium one, an 18-inch rear wheel, a side stand on the footpeg bracket, three off-road ignition maps, a rear sprocket one tooth larger, off-road fork and shock valving with a shock spring one rate softer (fork springs the same) and less rigid upper engine hangers. The gearbox is the same five-speed close-ratio unit. It has no spark arrestor.

q: How is my bike different from its sister models? I never really understood the lineup.
topic: 2014-2015 FC models against the KTM SX-F
statement: The 2014-2015 Austrian-built Husqvarna FC models are the KTM SX-F of the same year with these differences: a polyamide composite subframe instead of aluminium, a left side panel that is also the airbox cover (sealed, where the KTM is vented), D.I.D DirtStar rims instead of Excel, a 20 mm rear axle on 2014 bikes (KTM 25 mm), two seat bolts hidden in the hand-holds, a handlebar switch for two ignition maps as standard, a muffler with extra sound-deadening screens, and white bodywork with its own tank and seat. From 2015 they carry Neken bars and the WP 4CS fork.

q: What sets my bike apart from the motocross version or the other models it's related to?
statement: Pre-2022 YZ125s pulled harder than the KTM 125SX below about 7,800-8,000 rpm and were easier to keep on the pipe; above 8,000 the KTM was described as night-and-day faster.

q: What sets my bike apart from the motocross version or the other models it's related to?
statement: The CRF150R makes about 23.5 hp at the crank (roughly 21 at the wheel). It has more torque than an 85 cc two-stroke and a smoother curve, but it is heavier, revs up and down quickly and is a race engine, not a trail engine: little flywheel and easy to stall.

q: How is my bike different from its sister models? I never really understood the lineup.
statement: The 2015 250 XC-F has the same engine and chassis as the 250 SX-F, with only a side-stand tab added to the frame. It adds a larger tank, the side stand, an 18-inch rear wheel, handguards and off-road suspension valving, on a six-speed semi-wide-ratio gearbox. The engine has a plain big-end bearing.

q: How is my bike different from its sister models? I never really understood the lineup.
statement: Of the 2016 two-strokes, the TE 250 is the livelier, with smooth, predictable power, less vibration and a lighter feel. The TE 300 pulls harder from the bottom and needs less clutch in slow going. Both feel planted and are less likely to deflect off roots and rocks than the 125. Both have a two-map switch on the bar.

q: Teach me a little about my bike. What did the factory change this year?
statement: 2015 450 SX-F changes: WP 4CS (four-chamber) fork on US bikes, 4.8 N/mm fork springs (was 5.0), a 20 mm front axle (was 25) with its offset moved 2 mm rearward (35 to 33 mm), a new linkage bell crank with a pull rod 2.5 mm longer, a shock 4 mm longer (rear seat height 5 mm lower), a forged one-piece frame cross tube, an orange frame, black Excel rims and Dunlop MX52 tyres. The engine is unchanged; the bike is 466 g lighter.

q: What was new on my bike for this model year?
statement: The 2013 250 SX-F got a new engine: bore up 2 mm and stroke down 2.5 mm, intake valves enlarged from 30.9 to 32.5 mm, die-cast cases, a plain-bearing rod, a 44 mm throttle body (was 42), a six-speed gearbox with a revised second gear, an exhaust that pulls out from the front, plus a new frame, swingarm and clamps, a 25 mm rear axle and bars 12 mm taller. This platform ran 2013-2015.

q: Teach me a little about my bike. What did the factory change this year?
statement: The CRF150R is a 149 cc liquid-cooled four-stroke with a carburettor, a light flywheel and a five-speed close-ratio gearbox; engine and gearbox oil are separate. It was introduced for 2007, got a needle change for 2008 and, for 2012, a new cylinder head, piston, camshaft and accelerator-pump circuit. The small-wheel bike runs 17/14-inch wheels with a 32.8 in seat and about 185 lb wet; the big-wheel (Expert) runs 19/16-inch wheels, a 34.1 in seat, about 187 lb and slightly firmer valving. Fork travel is 10.8 in and both ends are fully adjustable. The tank holds 1.11 gallons.

q: What was new on my bike for this model year?
statement: 2015 CRF450R changes: a revised head, a heat-treated piston, more flywheel inertia, a stronger gearbox, three engine maps on a handlebar button, a shorter exhaust with larger tubes, Kayaba PSF-2 fork (compression in one leg, rebound in the other, high- and low-speed adjusters on the caps), all shock adjusters on the reservoir, a 260 mm front disc and Dunlop MX52 tyres.

q: What was new on my bike for this model year?
statement: For 2014 the 250 XC-W got a redesigned reed housing with Boyesen reeds, an optimised ignition curve and cylinder head with matching carburettor settings, a 4 Ah battery in place of the 3 Ah one for surer starting, a lighter chain guide, a front brake master cylinder with a smaller piston and new pads, and a stiffer, rib-free front fender. It keeps the PDS shock (335 mm travel) and 48 mm fork (300 mm), runs 60:1 premix, holds 2.6 gallons and weighs 225.1 lb without fuel.

q: Teach me a little about my bike. What did the factory change this year?
statement: The 2013 CRF450R was redesigned and restyled with twin mufflers, meant to move weight forward and centralise mass, an air fork and significant engine changes. It was briefly the lightest bike in the class and popular with amateur racers; critics faulted its handling and it later fell behind on horsepower.

q: What was new on my bike for this model year?
statement: The 2019 FC 450 took the 2019 KTM changes: a frame 10% stiffer in torsion, a head 15 mm lower and 1 lb lighter, Pankl gears on the same ratios, radiators 12 mm lower with 20% more coolant, and a two-piece subframe in place of the three-piece. It keeps the Magura clutch, has Pro Taper bars in a new bend, and its muffler has a restrictor cone worth about 1 hp against the KTM's straight-through one.

q: Teach me a little about my bike. What did the factory change this year?
statement: The 2017 250 SX was new: an overhauled engine on the same 66.4 x 72 mm bore and stroke (new cases, ports, head and clutch), a 38 mm Mikuni TMX carburettor in place of the Keihin, the lighter frame with 20% more torsional stiffness and a wheelbase 10 mm shorter, a shock 12 mm shorter and the WP AER 48 air fork. 211 lb without fuel; list price $7,699 (2018: $7,899, with the carburettor angle changed from 12 to 7 degrees and an orange frame).

q: Teach me a little about my bike. What did the factory change this year?
statement: All 2015 TE and FE models got a new headlight, front mask and motocross-style front fender, revised black CNC triple clamps, an extra subframe screw on the left for a better airbox seal, stronger handguards as standard and a firmer seat. The four-strokes got new O-rings on the oil-pump suction screen. The TE 250 and TE 300 got shorter starter gearing, a lighter 3 Ah battery and a new inner clutch-cover gasket; the TE 250 also had its power-valve opening point raised 200 rpm with improved carburation. The FE 350 got a lighter clutch basket. No model-specific changes were listed for the FE 450 or FE 501.

q: What was new on my bike for this model year?
statement: For 2018 the 150 XC-W got updated fork and shock settings, an updated 38 mm Mikuni, a new CDI unit, stiffer radiators and new radiator guards. Claimed weight 201.7 lb, list price $8,199. It has a 58 x 54.5 mm engine, six-speed gearbox, 2.6-gallon tank and a 37.8 in seat.

q: What was new on my bike for this model year?
statement: 2019 TC 250 changes: a two-piece composite airbox and subframe, the stiffer 2019 frame with aluminium head stays, welded aluminium silencer brackets in place of rubber, a new Pro Taper bar bend, and a tamer delivery with the same peak power as the KTM. 212 lb; list price $8,299. Husqvarna said the Magura slave-seal problem was fixed for 2020.

q: What was new on my bike for this model year?
statement: 2017 350 SX-F changes: WP AER 48 air fork (3.6 lb lighter than the 4CS), a stiffer top clamp, a 42 N/mm shock spring (was 48), a handlebar multi-switch with two maps, launch control and traction control, a longer rear brake pedal with milder pads, aluminium head stays and an hour meter. 221 lb; list price $9,199.

q: Teach me a little about my bike. What did the factory change this year?
topic: FE 450 and a tester 2016 updates and specs
statement: For 2016 the FE 450 and a tester got a 22 mm front axle in place of the 26 mm one, 22 mm offset triple clamps with revised front geometry, new brakes (260 mm front, 220 mm rear), lighter spokes, a lighter clutch basket and a grippier seat cover. Both have a six-speed gearbox, DDS clutch with Brembo hydraulics, a 48 mm WP 4CS fork (11.8 in travel), a linkage shock (13 in), a 2.25-gallon tank and a 38.2 in seat. The maker lists 53 hp and 248.7 lb without fuel for the FE 450 and 58 hp and 249.8 lb for the a tester. List prices $9,999 and $10,199.

q: What was new on my bike for this model year?
statement: All 2015 KTM XC models got a 4CS fork 8 mm longer with a new hydraulic stop, new pistons and a 20 N/mm chamber spring (was 18), a re-valved shock with 4 mm more shaft travel, new linkage geometry, a 22 mm front axle in place of the 26 mm one (moved back 2 mm), a lighter rear sprocket and a frame with a machined cross tube. The two-strokes and the 250 and 350 XC-F got a lighter clutch basket; the 250 and 350 XC-F also got new clutch springs. The 450 XC-F stayed a five-speed SOHC; the 250 and 350 are six-speed DOHC engines.

q: Tell me about my bike. What's the basic layout and specs I should know?
statement: The 2017 TX 125 is a 124.8 cc (54.0 x 54.5 mm) kick-start two-stroke with a six-speed gearbox and hydraulic clutch. It uses the WP Xplor 48 fork with preload adjusters (300 mm travel) and a linkage shock (330 mm), a 10-litre (2.64-gallon) tank, a 960 mm seat, a 21-inch front and 18-inch rear wheel, and weighs 92.2 kg dry.

q: Tell me about my bike. What's the basic layout and specs I should know?
statement: The 350 SX-F was new for 2011: a fuel-injected, electric-start 350 in the steel linkage frame that replaced PDS that year (5 mm lower and 15 mm wider at the pegs), with a steel clutch basket, a 1.98 gal tank and an optional kickstarter. List price $8,499.

q: I'm new to this bike. Give me the rundown on what it is.
statement: The 2019 250 XC and 300 XC are carburetted two-stroke cross-country racers built on the SX: the stiffer 2019 frame, a subframe 40 mm longer, an axle slot 5 mm longer, radiators 12 mm lower, a new pipe and silencer and new carburettor settings, with electric start, a six-speed close-ratio gearbox, a hydraulic clutch, the WP AER 48 air fork, a linkage shock, a 2.65 gal tank, an 18 in rear wheel, hand guards, a side stand and a slightly heavier flywheel than the SX. The 250 XC listed at $9,399.

q: Tell me about my bike. What's the basic layout and specs I should know?
statement: The carbureted CRF450X is a 449 cc Unicam four-valve single (96 x 62 mm, 12.0:1) fed by a 40 mm Keihin flat-slide carburettor with a throttle position sensor. It has electric and kick start, a five-speed wide-ratio gearbox, a sealed 520 chain, a twin-spar aluminium frame, a 47 mm Showa cartridge fork and linkage Showa shock with 12.4 in of travel at each end, an 18-inch rear wheel and Honda's non-adjustable steering damper. Seat height 37.9 in, 1.9-gallon tank, 269 lb curb weight, $8,699 list in 2017.

q: Tell me about my bike. What's the basic layout and specs I should know?
statement: The 2013 WR250F is a five-titanium-valve DOHC 249 cc engine (12.5:1) with a 37 mm Keihin FCR flat-slide, electric start with a kick backup and a five-speed gearbox, with a 48 mm Kayaba cartridge fork (11.8 in travel) and linkage shock (12.2 in). Seat height 38.6 in, 2.1-gallon tank, 254 lb wet by the US spec. US list price $6,990.

q: Tell me about my bike. What's the basic layout and specs I should know?
statement: KTM 450 SX-F milestones: 2011 rising-rate linkage replaces the linkless PDS shock on a new steel frame (still carburetted); 2013 new single-cam fuel-injected engine with plain bearings and a new chassis; 2015 WP 4CS fork on US bikes, 20 mm front axle and Excel rims; 2016 all-new lighter platform (227 lb); 2017 WP AER 48 air fork, traction control and a two-map switch (222 lb); 2019 new frame 10% stiffer in torsion with a cylinder head 15 mm lower.

q: Tell me about my bike. What's the basic layout and specs I should know?
statement: The 2018 250 XC-F is a 249.9 cc DOHC four-valve engine (78 x 52.3 mm, 14.4:1) with Keihin fuel injection and a six-speed gearbox. It uses the WP AER air fork (310 mm travel) and a linkage shock (300 mm), holds 2.3 gallons, has a 960 mm seat and a listed dry weight of 218.7 lb.

q: I'm new to this bike. Give me the rundown on what it is.
statement: The CRF250X is a 249 cc Unicam four-valve single (78 x 52.2 mm) with a 37 mm Keihin flat-slide carburettor and throttle position sensor, electric and kick start, a five-speed wide-ratio gearbox, 14/53 gearing on a 520 chain, a twin-spar aluminium frame, a 47 mm Showa cartridge fork (12.4 in travel) and Pro-Link Showa shock (12.3 in), and an 18-inch rear wheel. The tank holds 1.9 gallons including a 0.4-gallon reserve. Seat height 37.7 in, 254 lb curb weight, $7,410 list in 2016.

q: What suspension settings did test riders settle on for my bike?
statement: On the 2017 450 XC-F the air fork has more small-bump compliance than the 2016 4CS. Testers added 1 psi and a few clicks of fork compression for balance, added up to five clicks of shock low-speed compression for the motocross track, and ran 103-108 mm of rider sag.

q: What suspension settings did test riders settle on for my bike?
statement: On the 2017 FX 350 the air fork is plush off-road and a little soft for motocross. To stop it bottoming, raise the air pressure, stiffen the clicker, or both. Check the pressure with the supplied gauge before every ride.

q: I like learning how other people set these up. What did the testers run for suspension on mine?
statement: A magazine test crew's 2012-2013 350 SX-F setup: fork stock 0.48 kg/mm springs, 375 cc oil in 2012 and 390 cc in 2013 (lower it 10 cc for riders under 175 lb), compression 15 clicks out, rebound 15 out, legs 5 mm up. Shock 5.7 kg/mm spring (5.4 for lighter riders), 105 mm sag, high-speed compression 2 turns out, low-speed 15 clicks out, rebound 15 out.

q: What suspension settings did test riders settle on for my bike?
statement: A magazine test crew's 2014 YZ450F setup: fork stock 4.9 N/mm springs, 335 cc oil (pros add 10 cc), compression 11 clicks out (stock 9), rebound 8 out, legs 4 mm up. Shock stock 58 N/mm spring, 105 mm sag (stock 100), high-speed compression 2 turns out (stock 1-1/2), low-speed 12 clicks out, rebound 9 out (stock 14). Rear sprocket 50 in place of 49.

q: I like learning how other people set these up. What did the testers run for suspension on mine?
statement: On the 2015 250 XC-F the 4CS fork's adjuster works mainly on mid-speed damping and needs 3-5 clicks before a change is felt, while 1-2 clicks on the shock are noticeable. For motocross, run it stock (riders under 165 lb may want softer springs). For off-road, go 3-5 clicks softer on fork compression and rebound, match the shock softer and take half a turn off the shock's high-speed compression. Sag is 100-105 mm. For tight racing add two rear teeth or drop one on the countershaft.

q: I like learning how other people set these up. What did the testers run for suspension on mine?
statement: A magazine test crew's 2019 250 SX-F setup: fork air 136 psi (stock 149; lighter riders 132 or less), compression 28 clicks out (stock 15), rebound 17 out (stock 15), legs at the third line. Shock stock 42 N/mm spring (45 over 185 lb), 107 mm sag (stock 105; it cured a front-end oversteer in sand), high-speed compression 2-3/4 turns out (stock 2), low-speed 15 clicks out, rebound 11 out (stock 15).

q: I like learning how other people set these up. What did the testers run for suspension on mine?
statement: Testers ran about 106 mm of sag on the 2019 CRF450X and found the stock springs right for riders of about 170-210 lb. For a plusher ride they went 4-6 clicks softer on compression at both ends. On the fork, bleeding the air to a slight negative pressure and opening rebound 1-2 clicks helped small-bump feel.

q: I like learning how other people set these up. What did the testers run for suspension on mine?
statement: A magazine test crew's 2013 CRF250R setup: fork stock 0.46 kg/mm springs, 363 cc oil, compression 6 clicks out (stock 7), rebound 9 out (stock 11), legs flush, steering damper 7 out (stock 9). Shock 5.3 kg/mm spring, 104 mm sag (100 for heavier riders), high-speed compression 1-3/4 turns out (stock 2), low-speed 8 clicks out, rebound 9 out (stock 11).

q: What suspension settings did test riders settle on for my bike?
statement: A magazine test crew's 2018 CRF450R setup: fork stock springs, compression and rebound 12 clicks out (pros 10 and 13, vets and novices 13 and 13), legs raised to the second line; 10 cc more oil is the cheap fix for harshness near the bottom of the stroke. Shock stock 56 N/mm spring (light riders 54), 107 mm sag, high-speed compression 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 turns out, low-speed 10 clicks out, rebound 7 out. A shock link 1.5 mm longer than stock was the testers' pick.

q: What suspension settings did test riders settle on for my bike?
topic: FC 350 2019 tester fork and shock settings
statement: A magazine crew's 2019 FC 350 setup. Fork (AER 48): 140 psi (stock 152), compression 25 clicks out (stock 15), rebound 17 out (stock 15), legs at the third line. Shock: 42 N/mm spring (45 N/mm for riders over 185 lb), race sag 105 mm (stock 110), high-speed compression 1-3/4 turns out (stock 2), low-speed compression 15 clicks out, rebound 10 out (stock 15). Gearing: a 51-tooth rear, some testers 52.

q: What suspension settings did test riders settle on for my bike?
statement: A magazine test crew's 2016 CRF250R setup: fork inner chamber 156 psi (stock 174), outer 8 psi (stock 12), balance 156 psi (stock 170), compression 6 clicks out, rebound 18 out (stock 24), legs flush with the top clamp (start 5 mm up and lower them for rough or fast tracks). Shock 5.3 kg/mm spring, 105 mm sag (100 for heavier riders), high-speed compression 2-3/4 turns out (stock 3), low-speed 10 clicks out, rebound 6 out (stock 8). Use the glyphs on the fork-cap sticker to be sure each pressure goes in the right valve.

q: I like learning how other people set these up. What did the testers run for suspension on mine?
statement: An independent tester's 2016 450 XC-F setup: rider sag 103-108 mm; off-road, fork compression and rebound 12-13 clicks out with the shock's compression about 5 clicks softer than standard; on a motocross track, up to 5 clicks more low-speed compression at the rear.

q: I like learning how other people set these up. What did the testers run for suspension on mine?
statement: On the 2016 350 XC-F testers left the 4CS fork clickers near standard and raised the fork oil level to cut bottoming. The shock went 1-4 clicks softer for trail and firmer for the track, with ride height settled at 103 mm of sag.

q: I like learning how other people set these up. What did the testers run for suspension on mine?
statement: A magazine test crew's 2016 KX450F shock setup: stock 52 N/mm spring, 105 mm race sag, high-speed compression 2-1/4 turns out (stock 1-3/4), low-speed 15 clicks out (stock 13), rebound 11 out (stock 12). Stock gearing was kept.

q: What suspension settings did test riders settle on for my bike?
statement: Testers ran the 2014 350 XC-F's 4CS fork at 10-12 clicks out on both compression and rebound with 105 mm of rear sag. The fork is firm over rocks and roots and good on a motocross track; the shock spring is a little light for riders of 180 lb and up. A 52-tooth rear sprocket was tried and dropped: it made the engine lug and flame out, so stock 13/50 stayed.

q: What suspension settings did test riders settle on for my bike?
statement: A magazine test crew's 2019 KX450 fork setup: stock 5.0 N/mm springs are soft for aggressive riders; vets ran an effective 5.1 (one 5.0 and one 5.2 spring), fast riders the optional 5.2, light riders stock. Compression 14 clicks out, rebound 12 out, fork legs up to 2 mm up. Light or slower riders added oil in 5 cc steps to both legs to stop bottoming.

q: Anything this bike is known to wear out or break that I should keep an eye on?
statement: Tester notes on the 2017-2018 XC-W: the rear spring rate matters more than usual on the PDS shock (too heavy a rider and it squats, too light and it is unstable), the fork seals needed replacing after muddy rides, the lithium battery wants a short tap of the starter about 20 seconds before cranking on a cold morning, and the brakes have less outright bite and more control than the earlier bikes.

q: What are the known weak spots on my bike?
topic: spokes, brake spring, oil check (carb era)
statement: Spokes next to the rim lock loosen quickly in break-in; the rear brake pedal spring falls off or breaks (turn it round or fit a Honda spring); there is no oil sight glass, so check via the 8 mm weep bolt behind the brake spring.

q: Anything this bike is known to wear out or break that I should keep an eye on?
topic: 350 XC-F 2016 stalling, cold starts and other findings
statement: The 2016 350 XC-F stalls easily at closed throttle unless the idle is set carefully, and a correct idle also helps cold starting (it may need a first button push and a few seconds for the battery to wake up). The clutch overheats if it is slipped in too high a gear. A test bike leaked oil at the ignition-cover set screw until it was sealed. The fuel hose is exposed and the bike needs a skid plate.

q: What are the known weak spots on my bike?
statement: On the 2018 TC 250: sprocket bolts loosen and spokes need constant checking; the fuel cap sticks; the fork's air-side bleeder strips easily; the fork air valve is hard to reach; tie-down hooks can crimp the front brake hose. For the abrupt power, use the bar map switch and turn the power-valve adjuster clockwise (it takes a square-drive tool). An aftermarket pipe and silencer added about 3 hp from 7,000 to 9,500 rpm.

q: Anything this bike is known to wear out or break that I should keep an eye on?
statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2014-2018 YZ250F: early bikes had water-pump shaft, gear-stop roller and connecting-rod failures, which Yamaha addressed with stronger parts in 2015, 2016 and 2017; the 250 mm front brake on 2014-2015 bikes is weak (oversize disc), while the 270 mm brake from 2016 is strong but grabby; the airbox fasteners on 2015-2016 bikes fall out or snag; the wrap-around exhaust is hard to remove; the intake is loud and its backfire screen restricts flow (an aftermarket cage and filter kit); the shock hops under hard braking (soften low-speed, adjust high-speed); the bars have a tall, swept bend many riders replace; and the 2016 rear disc could warp.

q: What are the known weak spots on my bike?
statement: Tester complaints on the carburetted 2010-2013 YZ250F: a short powerband that makes gearing hard to get right, fork mid-stroke harshness (cured with oil level), a shock that hops under hard braking (back off high-speed compression and soften low-speed), side panels that barely take a number, and on 2012-2013 bikes black rims that scratch quickly. Durability was rated very good.

q: Anything this bike is known to wear out or break that I should keep an eye on?
statement: Tester complaints on the YZ250X: fourth and fifth are too tall for tight trail, the tank is too small for a 40-mile loop (an oversize tank is the fix), the clutch springs are too soft, and converting to a 19 in rear wheel for motocross means lacing a 19 in rim to the stock hub with YZ250 spokes.

q: Anything this bike is known to wear out or break that I should keep an eye on?
statement: Common CRF150R problems: stalling (cured with flywheel weight, jetting work or an auto-clutch), hard kick-starting and a hanging idle after it has sat on pump fuel (clean the carburettor), and a harsh ride for trail use (springs for the rider, sag, then clickers one change at a time). Early valve and top-end failures are mostly put down to neglected maintenance.

q: What are the known weak spots on my bike?
statement: Findings on a 2015 250 XC-F: fork stiction on hard ground (oiling the seals and bleeding the air helped), a stock rear tyre that struggles on hard surfaces, fragile handguards that discolour, a touchy rear brake, no skid plate, and a loud muffler with no spark arrestor.

q: Anything this bike is known to wear out or break that I should keep an eye on?
topic: spokes, brake spring, oil check (carb era)
statement: Spokes next to the rim lock loosen quickly in break-in; the rear brake pedal spring falls off or breaks (turn it round or fit a Honda spring); there is no oil sight glass, so check via the 8 mm weep bolt behind the brake spring.

q: What are the known weak spots on my bike?
statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2017-2019 CRF450R: the clutch judder spring and plate break and the clutch fades (remove the judder parts and add a full friction plate; add stiffer springs sparingly), the radiator fins dent within about 20 hours and the bike boils over when raced hard (radiator sleeves; a 1.6-2.0 cap in place of the stock 1.1), the front brake is weak at a light pull and grabby when squeezed (better fluid, remove the disc guards), the fork is harsh and dives, and the bike shakes its head on fast rough straights (more sag, around 107-108 mm; some riders refit a steering damper). The airbox side vents let in dirt and water.

q: Anything this bike is known to wear out or break that I should keep an eye on?
statement: Tester findings on the 2019 250 XC: brake pedal return springs wore out repeatedly (an aftermarket spring kit or the earlier round spring), and the fuel tap leaked into the carburettor when turned off; leaving it on reserve stopped it.

q: What are the known weak spots on my bike?
topic: RM-Z250 weak points and fixes from race tests
statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2019-generation RM-Z250: clutch friction plates wear fast and it slips within a few hours of hard use (stiffer springs), the fork is supercross-stiff, the gearbox is notchy when shifted under load, the front brake is weak and fades, and it is the heaviest and least powerful bike in the class with no electric start. On the other side, testers logged 50-plus hours a year on these bikes since 2019 with no serious failures.

q: What are the known weak spots on my bike?
statement: On the 2019 FC 350: the airbox is restrictive (drill five 1-1/4 inch holes in the cover behind the filter); the muffler has a restrictor cone (a straight-through muffler, or a full aftermarket system for about 2 hp); the rear sprocket bolts do not seat fully and loosen (lap the tapers and keep checking); spokes still loosen despite new nipples; the fork guards only cover the front, so fork seals wear; and the new two-piece subframe is less supple than the old one. The diaphragm-spring clutch proved durable.

q: How would you describe the power delivery on my bike?
statement: The 2012-2016 250 SX makes about 50 hp on a magazine dyno, about 5 hp more than the YZ250 of the same years, and weighs 217-218 lb. It has little torque right off the bottom and snaps hard just before the midrange.

q: What's the engine character like on this bike? How's it best ridden?
statement: The counterbalanced 2017 250 XC-W is very smooth, with most two-stroke vibration gone. It has strong low-rpm torque, forgives a lazy gear choice and revs out cleanly. Testers noticed only a faint midrange hitch in the carburation. It uses fuel quickly.

q: How would you describe the power delivery on my bike?
topic: 450 XC-F 2017 weight, range, speed and engine feel
statement: A 2017 450 XC-F weighed 241 lb with a full 2.2-gallon tank and 230 lb without fuel, and listed at $10,099. It goes about 50 miles on a tank and runs into the limiter at 91 mph on stock gearing. The engine is torque-heavy and hooks up, and still revs freely on top. It stalls easily at small throttle openings if the clutch work is sloppy.

q: What's the engine character like on this bike? How's it best ridden?
statement: The 2019 WR450F weighed 258 lb without fuel on a magazine scale (262 lb claimed wet), about 20 lb more than a KTM 450 XC-F. With the throttle stop and inner muffler out it is still very quiet, with strong, smooth low-end and far less intimidating power than the YZ450F or YZ450FX. It can be hard to start: it wants a small, exact amount of throttle, and long cranking should be avoided to protect the battery.

q: What's the engine character like on this bike? How's it best ridden?
statement: The 2015 KX450F is smooth off the bottom and strong in the middle; testers felt the 2014 pulled harder down low and faster riders preferred the 2014 powerband. It ranked fourth in the class for peak power.

q: How would you describe the power delivery on my bike?
statement: Measured on a dyno, the 2020 450 SX-F's vented airbox cover added about 0.25 hp at 9,000 rpm, 1 hp at 10,000 rpm, 1.1 hp at 11,000 rpm, 1 hp at peak and about 0.5 lb-ft throughout versus the solid cover.

q: How would you describe the power delivery on my bike?
statement: The pre-2017 FE 501 starts easily and makes immediate, smooth power with a very strong bottom and midrange; it is a short-shift engine and vibrates more than the 450. The six-speed has a very low first and an overdrive sixth for fast transfers.

q: What's the engine character like on this bike? How's it best ridden?
statement: The 2018-2019 KX250 makes about 40 hp, roughly 4 hp less than the Austrian 250s. It builds slowly off the bottom, has a bump in the middle and keeps pulling without falling off; riders often needed two downshifts into a corner where other 250s need one.

q: What's the engine character like on this bike? How's it best ridden?
statement: The 2014 250 XC pulls from low rpm and is very tractable for a 250 two-stroke, with more snap off the bottom than the 300. It does not rev as high on a motocross track as riders expect. The adjustable power valve changes the hit slightly. The clutch pull is light and resists fade. Stock gearing worked everywhere.

q: How would you describe the power delivery on my bike?
statement: The 2016 XC-F models share frame, engine and mapping with the SX-F motocross bikes and add an 18-inch rear wheel, handguards, off-road suspension settings, a 2.25-gallon tank (1.85 on the SX-F) and a side stand. The 250 XC-F gained torque and bottom-end with a smoother move into the midrange and is strong on tight, technical ground. The 350 XC-F has a wide powerband with a strong bottom but needs more shifting on a track. The 450 XC-F has heavy bottom-end torque and is best ridden a gear higher than usual; ridden like a motocross bike it wears the rider out.

q: What do the different map settings on my bike actually do?
statement: Testers on 2020-2022 bikes used map 2 (aggressive) on soft, loamy tracks and day to day, and map 1 (mellow) on hard-packed, slippery, wet or very technical tracks; on the 2022 FC 250 every tester ran map 2 because it adds power at every point in the curve.

q: What do the different map settings on my bike actually do?
topic: FX 350 2018 map switch, traction control and launch control
statement: The 2018 FX 350's bar switch chooses between two maps, turns traction control on or off and arms launch control for starts. Traction control compares throttle position with how fast the revs are rising and trims power when they climb too quickly. The bike is a 349.7 cc DOHC six-speed (semi-close ratios) with a Magura hydraulic clutch, the WP AER 48 fork (310 mm travel), a linkage shock (300 mm), a 2.25-gallon tank and a 960 mm seat, and weighs 221.8 lb without fuel.

q: Can you explain the maps and electronics on my bike and when to use each?
statement: The fuel-injected 2010-2013 CRF250R needs no jetting. Idle is set on a click adjuster with about 90 clicks of range; the base setting is 60 clicks out and one click is about 100 rpm.

q: Can you explain the maps and electronics on my bike and when to use each?
statement: The 2014 KX450F comes with three plug-in couplers: green (stock), black (mellow) and white (aggressive). On the dyno the white coupler showed no peak gain over stock and the black one gave up about 1 hp. Launch control leaves power alone below 7,000 rpm and trims it progressively above, works in first and second and switches off in third. Testers used it on hard dirt and concrete, not in loam.

q: Can you explain the maps and electronics on my bike and when to use each?
statement: Carbureted Husqvarna TC models have a handlebar map switch (map 1 aggressive, map 2 mellow) that testers found hidden under the throttle cables and hard to read.

q: If I wanted a little more out of the engine, what really works on my bike?
statement: Owners re-time the YZ250 governor by swapping two 1.0 mm thrust washers for 0.8 mm YZ250X washers and removing one, cutting spring preload by about 1.4 mm so the valve opens earlier; it fills the off-idle dip but needs a leaner power jet (#35 reported).

q: What mods are actually worth doing on this bike?
statement: A thin-plate friction pack (more discs in the stock basket) is sold for 2013-2026 KTM 450 SX-Fs with a claimed 25% more torque capacity and 10% lighter pull. A complete kit with a steel-pin hub, billet pressure plate and cover is sold for 2023+ 250/350 SX-F and FC models.

q: If I wanted a little more out of the engine, what really works on my bike?
statement: The stock grey throttle cam on 2020-2022 KTMs has a very long throw; testers fit the black quick-turn cam supplied with the bike.

q: If I wanted a little more out of the engine, what really works on my bike?
topic: TE 300 2019 fixes for the slow midrange
statement: Tested answers to the 2019 TE 300's slow low-to-mid power: a 51-tooth rear sprocket in place of the stock 50 (13/50 is the US gearing), holes drilled in the airbox, the stock map, the optional quick-turn throttle cam, and an aftermarket pipe, which filled the 7,000 rpm dip.

q: What's the upkeep like on this bike?
statement: Honda schedules fork oil every 9 races (about 22.5 hours). A suspension columnist services a hard-ridden practice bike every 10-15 hours, while a European suspension dealer quotes 20-40 hours depending on the bike; both say sand, hard riding and fast riders shorten it. Oil is usually the last thing to wear; bushings, seals, piston bands and shims go first. Signs: you keep going stiffer and slower on the clickers and they do less. Riding type: race and practice.

q: What's the chassis like on this bike? Any tricks to getting it to feel right?
topic: RM-Z450 handling and how to balance it
statement: The RM-Z450 has the sharpest turn-in of the 450s but is unstable at speed as delivered. The magazine recipe: lower the rear (the softer 2019-on spring, 105-110 mm sag and a 1 mm longer link), then slide the fork down to flush. That gives more room to tune compression, rebound and fork height. Its 2019 peak of 54.39 hp compared with 60.21 for the CRF450R, 57.51 YZ450F, 57.14 450 SX-F, 56.40 FC 450 and 55.86 KX450.

q: What's the chassis like on this bike? Any tricks to getting it to feel right?
statement: The carbureted KTM 250 power valve starts opening at about 5,600 rpm with stock preload and is fully open at about 7,900 rpm with the stock yellow inner spring. Each full turn of the preload screw moves the opening point about 150 rpm.

q: What's the chassis like on this bike? Any tricks to getting it to feel right?
topic: what moving the axle back does
statement: Moving the rear axle back makes the shock feel softer, because the swingarm has more leverage on it, so you may need more compression. It also lengthens the wheelbase and puts more weight on the front tire, which improves high-speed stability but can slow cornering. The 2019 swingarm was 5 mm longer than before.

q: How does my bike handle? What's it good and bad at?
statement: The 2017-2019 CRF450R turns in sharply but is loose mid-corner and at speed, and it is sensitive to front-to-rear balance: small changes in sag or fork height change it a lot. Testers removed the two rear tank bolts and two exhaust-to-subframe bolts to let the frame flex more.

q: How does my bike handle? What's it good and bad at?
statement: The 2019 FE 350 is sprung very soft and the fork dives under hard braking; stiffer springs are the first place to spend money. The stock dual-sport tyres limit handling, and the rim locks come uninstalled, so the wheels need balancing for road use.

q: What's the chassis like on this bike? Any tricks to getting it to feel right?
statement: The 2016 450 XC-F took the new, smaller and lighter chassis and engine at the same time as the 450 SX-F and performs identically on power: smooth, torquey, able to chug at low revs and pull away on the throttle. Its off-road valving has less high-speed compression and rebound damping than the SX-F, so it is plusher without wallowing, the 4CS fork is less harsh at the top of the stroke than earlier versions, and it still copes with a motocross track. A rubber-mounted bar cuts vibration. It is a lot of bike in tight woods, resists turning more than the 350 XC-F, and suits open terrain, desert and GP-style racing.

q: What's the chassis like on this bike? Any tricks to getting it to feel right?
statement: The 2011-2012 450 SX-F has a 63.5 degree steering head angle. It tracks accurately, is stable at speed and less twitchy than the PDS bikes, but will not turn as tightly as the sharpest-steering Japanese 450 of the time.

topic: aftermarket adjustable-offset clamps and stock clamp weight
statement: Every KTM, Husqvarna and GasGas motocross bike since 2016 (GasGas since 2021) uses 22 mm clamp offset. One aftermarket set adjusts to 21, 22, 23 or 24 mm and weighs 2,140 g with bar mounts, against 2,229 g for the stock 2026 clamps and 2,300 g for the factory split clamps.
